p7.vllm-arkitekturen.2: vLLM splits the work into a frontend that speaks HTTP and text, and an engine that only sees token ids and GPU memory.
p7.vllm-arkitekturen.20: sends the step to the workers
p7.vllm-arkitekturen.29: The engine works in steps: in each step the scheduler picks a batch, workers run a forward pass, and every active request gets (usually) one new token. In the code the three parts are called schedule(), execute_model() and update_from_output(). Then the next step begins. Everything else in this module is about how the steps get filled.
p7.en-requests-livscykel.2: Waiting: tokenized, waiting for a slot. The scheduler first checks the prefix cache, then whether there are free KV blocks.
p7.en-requests-livscykel.3: Running: gets tokens in every step. First prefill, possibly split into chunks, then one token per step.
p7.en-requests-livscykel.4: Preempted: if the KV blocks run out, a request is thrown out and its blocks are freed. It goes back into the queue and is recomputed later.
p7.en-requests-livscykel.5: Finished: stop token, stop string, max_tokens or cancelled. The blocks are freed but stay in the prefix cache until they’re needed for something else.
p7.problemet-fragmenterat-minne.2: Before vLLM, servers often reserved one contiguous memory region per request, large enough for the maximum length. But nobody knows in advance how long the response will be.
p7.problemet-fragmenterat-minne.3: The result was that most of the KV memory was reserved but empty. Fewer requests fit, the batches stayed small and the GPU ran idle.
p7.problemet-fragmenterat-minne.4: The PagedAttention paper (2023) measured that existing systems used only 20–40% of KV memory for actual tokens.
p7.pagedattention.2: vLLM splits KV memory into blocks of a fixed number of tokens (16 by default). Every sequence has a block table that translates logical blocks into physical ones, just like virtual memory in an operating system.
p7.pagedattention.3: A new block is allocated only when the previous one is full. The waste is at most one half-full block per sequence.
p7.pagedattention.4: The blocks don’t have to sit next to each other. The attention kernel looks them up through the block table.
p7.pagedattention.5: Blocks can be shared between sequences: the basis for prefix caching.
p7.pagedattention.6: kv_cache[layer] ≈ [2, num_blocks, 16, n_kv, d_h] slot = block_table[pos // 16] · 16 + pos % 16
p7.pagedattention.11: Block size is 4 here so you can see it. vLLM uses 16.
p7.prefix-caching.2: Every full block gets a hash of its contents and the hash of the previous block. Two requests with the same beginning therefore get the same hash chain.
p7.prefix-caching.3:
h₁ = hash(None, tokens[0:16])
h₂ = hash(h₁,   tokens[16:32])
h₃ = hash(h₂,   tokens[32:48])
p7.prefix-caching.4: When a new request arrives, the scheduler looks up the hashes in order. Blocks that hit are reused with a reference counter, and only the rest needs prefill.
p7.prefix-caching.5: System prompts, few-shot examples and long conversations, where every new turn starts with the whole history, thus become almost free to prefill again.
p7.prefix-caching.6: Only full blocks are cached. The blocks of finished requests stay in the cache and are evicted (LRU) only when memory is needed.
p7.continuous-batching.2: Static batching: a batch runs until the longest sequence is done. Slots for sequences that have finished sit empty.
p7.continuous-batching.3: Continuous batching: the scheduler decides the batch again in every step. A slot that frees up is filled immediately by the next request in the queue.
p7.continuous-batching.4: Because decode is memory-bound, a step costs almost the same no matter how many slots are in use. Every empty slot is therefore wasted capacity.
p7.continuous-batching.5: Simplified: 4 slots, prefill counts as one step, the number in the box is the request number.
p7.chunked-prefill-och-token.2: Every step has a budget: max_num_batched_tokens. The scheduler fills it in order:
p7.chunked-prefill-och-token.3: One token to every request in decode.
p7.chunked-prefill-och-token.4: The remaining budget to prefill, split into chunks if the prompt is too long.
p7.chunked-prefill-och-token.5: A long prompt of 5,000 tokens therefore takes three steps with max_num_batched_tokens = 2048 (2048 + 2048 + 904) instead of blocking everything at once. Decode requests get their token in every step, and ITL stays even.
p7.chunked-prefill-och-token.6: Prefill and decode in the same step also use the GPU better: prefill tokens give arithmetic work to a step that would otherwise mostly read memory.
p7.ett-steg-i-model-runner.1: One step in the model runner
p7.ett-steg-i-model-runner.2: vLLM does not pad the batch to [B, T]. All tokens from all requests are flattened into one long row, and metadata says where each request starts.
p7.ett-steg-i-model-runner.3: hidden [7, 4096] through all 32 layers logits [3, 128256] only logits_indices new ids [3]
p7.ett-steg-i-model-runner.4: Matmuls against the weights only see one tensor [N_tokens, 4096]. It makes no difference which request a row comes from. Only attention needs to know, and reads it from query_start_loc, seq_lens and block tables.
p7.ett-steg-i-model-runner.5: CUDA graphs: a decode step consists of hundreds of small kernel launches. vLLM records them as graphs for a number of fixed batch sizes and replays them, which removes most of the CPU overhead. --enforce-eager turns it off.
p7.ett-steg-i-model-runner.6: torch.compile fuses small operations (like RMSNorm and the residual add) into fewer kernels.
p7.samplern-och-structured.2: All requests in the batch are sampled at the same time. Each request’s parameters (temperature, top_p, seed) sit in tensors with shape [num_reqs], so the same kernels handle different settings per row.
p7.samplern-och-structured.3: Penalties lower the logits of tokens that have already appeared (repetition, presence, frequency).
p7.samplern-och-structured.4: Structured output (JSON schema, regex, grammar): a state machine knows which tokens are valid next. All others get logit −∞ before sampling. The model then cannot produce invalid JSON, whatever it “wants”. But if max_tokens cuts generation off in the middle of an object, you still get incomplete JSON: the constraint applies per token, not to the length.
p7.samplern-och-structured.5: The mask is a bitmask over the whole vocabulary, [num_reqs, 128256], computed on the CPU in parallel with the forward pass.
p7.tensor-parallelism.2: When the model does not fit on one GPU, or needs to run faster, every weight matrix is split across the GPUs.
p7.tensor-parallelism.3: Column parallel (qkv, gate_up): every GPU gets a slice of the output columns. Attention is split per head: with TP = 2 each GPU gets 16 query heads and 4 KV heads.
p7.tensor-parallelism.4: Row parallel (o_proj, down): each GPU holds a slice of the input and computes a partial sum. An all-reduce adds up the partial sums.
p7.tensor-parallelism.5: Two all-reduces per layer, that is 64 per forward pass in Llama-3-8B. It requires fast links such as NVLink, so TP is mostly used within one server.
p7.tensor-parallelism.6: Each GPU only holds the KV cache for its own heads. TP = 2 therefore gives twice as much total KV memory.
p7.pipeline-data-och-expert.2: Pipeline parallel: layers 0–15 on one GPU, 16–31 on the next. Little communication (only the stream between stages), works between servers. Needs several batches in flight so that every stage has work.
p7.pipeline-data-och-expert.3: Data parallel: the whole model is copied, and each copy takes its own requests. Best for throughput when the model fits.
p7.pipeline-data-och-expert.4: Expert parallel: for MoE. The experts are distributed, and tokens are sent where they belong with all-to-all.
p7.pipeline-data-och-expert.5: Rule of thumb: TP within a server, PP between servers, DP for more users, EP for large MoE models. Large deployments combine them.
p7.speculative-decoding.2: Decode is memory-bound: verifying 5 tokens in one forward pass costs almost as little as generating 1. Speculative decoding exploits that.
p7.speculative-decoding.3: A cheap proposal yields k tokens: a small draft model, n-grams from the prompt, EAGLE heads or the model’s own MTP layers.
p7.speculative-decoding.4: The large model runs all k positions in one pass, like a mini prefill.
p7.speculative-decoding.5: Proposals are accepted from the left until the first divergence. There the large model’s own token is used under greedy decoding; with sampling the replacement is instead drawn from the residual distribution normalize(max(0, p − q)), and that step is what gives exactly the target model’s distribution.
p7.speculative-decoding.6: With sampling, rejection sampling is used: accept with probability min(1, p/q). The outcome then has exactly the same distribution as the large model alone.
p7.flaggorna-och-vad-de-styr.1: The flags and what they control
p7.flaggorna-och-vad-de-styr.5: Share of the GPU memory vLLM takes. After weights and activations, the rest becomes KV blocks.
p7.flaggorna-och-vad-de-styr.7: Max context per sequence. At least one sequence of that length must fit in KV memory, or the server won’t start.
p7.flaggorna-och-vad-de-styr.9: Max number of requests in one step: the batch size in decode.
p7.flaggorna-och-vad-de-styr.11: Token budget per step. Controls the balance between TTFT and ITL via chunked prefill. A higher value reserves more memory for activations and leaves a smaller KV pool.
p7.flaggorna-och-vad-de-styr.13: Number of GPUs that split each layer. A TP size that does not divide the head count is rejected at startup; when TP exceeds the number of KV heads, the KV cache is replicated instead.
p7.flaggorna-och-vad-de-styr.15: Number of stages the layers are split into.
p7.flaggorna-och-vad-de-styr.19: awq, gptq, fp8 and more. Often read automatically from the model’s config.
p7.flaggorna-och-vad-de-styr.21: Prefix caching. On by default in newer versions.
p7.flaggorna-och-vad-de-styr.25: Draft model, n-gram, EAGLE or MTP, and the number of proposals k.
p7.flaggorna-och-vad-de-styr.27: Turns off CUDA graphs. For troubleshooting, costs performance.
p7.flaggorna-och-vad-de-styr.28: At startup vLLM logs how many tokens the KV cache holds and how many requests of the max length can run at the same time. It’s the calculator from module 6, worked out for real.
p7.hela-flodet.1: The whole flow, from HTTP to token
p7.testa-dig-sjalv-vllm.2: A request has 70 tokens in context. How many KV blocks does it use with block size 16, and how many slots end up empty?
p7.testa-dig-sjalv-vllm.3: 5 blocks (80 slots), of which 10 are empty in the last block.
p7.testa-dig-sjalv-vllm.4: Two users send the same 1,000-token system prompt. How much of the second request’s system prompt needs prefilling?
p7.testa-dig-sjalv-vllm.5: Only the last 8 tokens: 62 full blocks (992 tokens) are reused via the prefix cache, and the incomplete last block is recomputed.
p7.testa-dig-sjalv-vllm.6: Why does vLLM flatten the batch instead of padding to [B, T]?
p7.testa-dig-sjalv-vllm.7: Prompts and decode steps have completely different lengths. Padding would compute on empty positions. Matmuls do not care where a row comes from, and the attention kernel gets the boundaries via query_start_loc.
p7.testa-dig-sjalv-vllm.8: Why does TP = 16 work poorly for Llama-3-8B?
p7.testa-dig-sjalv-vllm.9: The model has only 8 KV heads, so they cannot be split across 16 GPUs without being duplicated. On top of that, each GPU’s matrices become so small that the all-reduce communication dominates.
p7.testa-dig-sjalv-vllm.10: What happens when the KV blocks run out in the middle of a generation?
p7.testa-dig-sjalv-vllm.11: The scheduler preempts a request, usually the most recently arrived one. Its blocks are freed and it is put back in the queue to be recomputed later.
